intended_object: The pole divisor (x)_∞ = Σ_{P : v_P(x) < 0} (−v_P(x))·P of an element x of a function field L, a finite separable extension of K(T). It is the negative part of the principal divisor div(x), which makes it effective. Inferred from the docstring, the name and how the library uses it (`finiteExtensionPoleDivisor_effective`, and its use as the divisor H in Riemann–Roch lower bounds).
explanation:
The definition takes the library's principal divisor D = div(x), a finitely supported function `FiniteExtensionPlace K L →₀ ℤ`. It keeps the places where D(v) < 0 and negates the result. At finite places, D(v) = `finitePlaceOrder`, the exponent of v in the fractional ideal (x). At places above infinity, D(v) is the same order for the prime over the infinite place. Zeros therefore get positive order and poles negative order: the library proves v.valuation x = exp(−order). So −(D restricted to {D < 0}) has value −v_P(x) at each pole and 0 everywhere else. That is exactly the textbook pole divisor (x)_∞, and it is effective.

For x = 0 the principal divisor is a junk value. The pole divisor of 0 is not a standard object anyway, so this is acceptable.

On generality: the definition lives on the library's own divisor type for finite separable extensions of RatFunc K. The `[Fintype K]` assumption comes from the ambient variable context; the body itself does not use it. Mathlib has no divisor theory or pole divisor for function fields, so no general counterpart exists. The construction is the natural one for the library's divisor group, so I do not count the setting as too narrow.
